situation: You've noticed that places like London or Bergen stay far milder in winter than Canadian places at similar latitudes, such as Labrador or the Prairies. You're asking what causes it. The popular answer credits the Gulf Stream, but how much of the gap comes from the ocean, how much from the winds, and how much from mountains and coastlines is genuinely disputed, and that split is the decisive uncertainty.

minds.title: The Ocean Mapper
minds.concern: Warm and cold sea currents move heat across the planet and shape coasts.
minds.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
minds.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea

minds.title: The Atmosphere Skeptic
minds.concern: Winds and air-mass movement, not just water, deliver or withhold warmth, and popular explanations often overcredit the sea.
minds.author: Dennis L. Hartmann

minds.title: The Tipping-Point Historian
minds.concern: The ocean circulation behind the warmth is a changeable system, so the answer matters for what could shift.
minds.author: Richard B. Alley

debate.speaker: The Ocean Mapper
debate.text: It's the Gulf Stream. A river of tropical water runs up the Atlantic and warms Europe's coast, while the Labrador side gets a cold current from the north. Same latitude, opposite plumbing. That's the whole story.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855), source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Too tidy. A current has to hand its heat to the air, and air has to carry it inland. The prevailing westerlies blow off the ocean onto Europe, but over Canada they blow off a cold continent. Wind direction may matter as much as water temperature.
debate.author: Dennis L. Hartmann
debate.basis: [Basis: Hartmann, Global Physical Climatology, source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Ocean Mapper
debate.text: Fair, but who warms that air? Water holds enormous heat. In autumn the Atlantic is still warm and releases it all winter. Canada's coast faces cold water and Arctic ice. The wind is the delivery truck; the ocean is the warehouse.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855), source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Nice image, but the warehouse is mostly local sea surface heat stored from summer, not Caribbean water arriving on schedule. I'd go further than the textbook here: much of the Gulf Stream's reputation may be inflated. Without it, the westerlies might still keep Europe fairly mild.
debate.author: Dennis L. Hartmann
debate.basis: [Basis: Hartmann, Global Physical Climatology, source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Tipping-Point Historian
debate.text: Careful about dismissing the ocean. Ice-core and sediment records show the North Atlantic circulation has shifted abruptly in the past, and the north got dramatically colder when it did. That doesn't prove it explains today's whole gap, but it shows the system can matter.
debate.author: Richard B. Alley
debate.basis: [Basis: Alley, The Two-Mile Time Machine, source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Abrupt past shifts are evidence of sensitivity, not of how much today's warmth depends on the current. A wobbly thermostat can still be a small part of the heating bill. Mountains also bend the jet stream, so the Rockies help push cold air down into eastern Canada.
debate.author: Dennis L. Hartmann
debate.basis: [Basis: Hartmann, Global Physical Climatology, source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Ocean Mapper
debate.text: Then I narrow my claim. Currents aren't the sole cause, but they set the sea surface temperatures that the winds pick up. Strip the warm water out and the westerlies would blow over a colder ocean. Wind and sea can't be separated that cleanly.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855), source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Tipping-Point Historian
debate.text: That's the useful disagreement. If winds do most of the work, a changing ocean current is a modest risk to Europe's winters. If the ocean matters more, it's a bigger one. The past shows large swings are possible; it doesn't settle which story is right.
debate.author: Richard B. Alley
debate.basis: [Basis: Alley, The Two-Mile Time Machine, source not verified online]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Agreed, and I'll concede one thing. Ocean heat transport is real and I shouldn't wave it away. But for the plain question of why Europe beats Canada in winter, I'd still start with where the wind comes from and what it crosses.
debate.author: Dennis L. Hartmann
debate.basis: [Basis: Hartmann, Global Physical Climatology, source not verified online]

clearer: The main insight is that the warm-Europe puzzle has several linked causes: wind direction (westerlies off an ocean versus off a continent), heat the sea stores in summer and releases in winter, mountains that steer the jet stream, and ocean currents that shape sea temperatures. What remains disputed is how large the Gulf Stream's share is compared with the winds and mountains. One thing to reflect on is whether you were hoping for a single cause, and how you feel about a layered answer. Note that the book sources are not verified online here, so their ideas are paraphrased cautiously.
dependsOn: If you want the simplest accurate answer, say that prevailing westerlies carry heat stored in the Atlantic over Europe, while Canada's winds come off a cold continent, and that warm and cold currents add to the contrast. If you care mainly about how the gap could change, the share of the effect due to ocean circulation becomes the key fact, because a larger share means a weakening current would matter more. To learn that share, look for climate-model experiments that remove ocean heat transport or mountains and compare the winter temperature changes over Europe and Canada.
